newsitem.title: CHINA: China hints at delays in sailings to Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: China hints at delays in sailings to Taiwan.

text.p: China was tightlipped on Friday about the start of direct shipping links with its rival Taiwan, appearing to try to play down a trade breakthrough seen by senior leaders as too little.

Officials of Chinese shipping lines that have won permission from Taipei authorities to begin direct sailings across the Taiwan strait held out little hope of lifting anchor before the weekend at the earliest.
"No ship will go today, although it is hard to speak now for tomorrow or Sunday," said an official of Xiamen Shipping Company.
The company's Sheng Da vessel was waiting in Xiamen port for the official green light to set sail, port officials said.

The vessel has won approval from officials of the Ministry of Communications in Beijing to begin direct sailings to Taiwan's huge southern port of Kaohsiung, but it has yet to receive official departure documents.

"As soon as these are received the vessel can load up and be on its way within about two hours," said one official at the port of Xiamen, which faces Taiwan. "But up to now we have not yet received any order."
Shipping line officials voiced nervousness at the delays.
"We don't know when the direct shipping will begin, it was arranged by officials at high levels," said the Xiamen Shipping official.
"The ship would go at once as the order is issued, but we are not sure when the ship can go," he said.
"We are very worried," he said but declined to comment further.

Taiwan issued permits to Chinese shipping lines several days ago, breaking a ban on direct links with China that had been in place since its Nationalist rulers fled into exile on the island after being defeated by the communists in a civil war in 1949.
Beijing, which sees Taiwan as rebel-held province that eventually must be brought under its sovereignty, has been pressing for years for Taiwan to end its ban.
But since Taiwan agreed to relax restrictions, Beijing appears to have dragged its feet, diplomats said.

China waited to issue licences to Taiwan shipping lines for direct sailings until Thursday, the final possible day under a mainland law mandating that Beijing act on such applications within 45 days of receiving them.
Local officials in Xiamen said they were under orders from Beijing to play down the first direct sailings.
"China has always wanted three direct links with Taiwan -- shipping, mail and trade," said one diplomat.
"But after all these years they have only managed to get this single one, and I think there is a feeling among the leaders that this is too little," he said. "It doesn't give them enough face."
The direct sailings will only begin under restrictions from Taipei forbidding direct cargo exchanges -- thus upholding its ban on direct mainland links.
Mainland cargoes will not be allowed to enter Taiwan customs but can be processed at Kaohsiung's new "offshore transshipment centre" for onward passage to third countries.
Likewise, Taiwan cargoes at Kaohsiung cannot be put aboard ships planning to cross directly to the Chinese mainland.
